notes: greedy from the largest Fibonacci number (1, 2, 3, 5, ...) not above n, digits as text, leading zeros dropped: the table 0..20 exactly as the Python entry's; the form of an arbitrary integer shown for 100, 1000, 10^6, 2^64 and 10^30 (growing ints, 144 digits), each read back to n by from_zeckendorf and checked for adjacent 1s (forms checked in Python); every n 0..10000 round-trips with no adjacent 1s

title: Zero to the zero power
notes: 0 ^ 0 is 1 in every kind, both modes: the task's x = 0, y = 0, z = x ^ y (z= 1); int, growing int (a zero made from 2 ^ 100, held compiled as crow_runtime::int::Int), float (0.0 ^ 0.0, (-0.0) ^ 0.0, mixed int/float), decimal (0.00, and of 50 digits), fraction, tensor .^ — each shown with its answer's kind; also NaN ^ 0.0 and infinity ^ 0.0 are 1 (IEEE pow) and -0.0 ^ 0.0 is -1 (a power binds tighter than a leading minus). The spec names no rule for 0 ^ 0 (section 4's ^ is the power; ints exact and growing, a negative int power stops, decimals and fractions exact by an int power — a float exponent on them is refused 'an exact number's power is by an int', in the compiler's words only), and the header says so. Note: a helper taking the value itself saw ints as floats (a function called with an int and a float takes floats: spec section 1, by design), so the table's text and kind are read at each call site

title: Zhang-Suen thinning algorithm
notes: the image a list of rows of 0/1 (read from text rows, 1 or # black); each round the two passes, each noting every black pixel with eight neighbours meeting conditions (0)-(4) and then whitening them all, until a round whitens nothing; shown as ASCII art (# and .): the task's 10x32 image thins exactly to the Python entry's output, and the description's 18x59 example thins to the thinned image the description shows (compared in the program: true); also six seeded random images (a solid block among them) agree with the Python entry's algorithm in both modes

title: Zsigmondy numbers
notes: Zs(n, a, b) as a^n - b^n with, for each m < n, the common part with a^m - b^m divided out until none is left (gcd only, no factoring), in growing ints: the ten radix pairs for n = 1..20 exactly as the Python/Raku entries, n = 21..30 (past 64 bits for a = 5, 6, 7) and the 100th of each pair (a^100 - b^100 up to 85 digits); all checked in Python against an independent cyclotomic method (Phi_n(a, b) less its largest prime of n) for n up to 60 and 100; the task's own definition (the largest coprime divisor, every divisor tried by trial division) checked in the program for n up to 10: true
